text: Whole-genome resequencing of extreme phenotypes in collared flycatchers highlights the difficulty of detecting quantitative trait loci in natural populations MARTY KARDOS,* ANNA QVARNSTR €OM§ and HANS ELLEGREN* *Department of Evolutionary Biology, Evolutionary Biology Centre (EBC), Uppsala University, Norbyv€agen 18D, Uppsala 75236, Sweden, †Department of Biosciences, University of Helsinki, PO Box 65, Helsinki 00014, Finland, ‡Centre for Biodiversity Dynamics, Department of Biology, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim 7491, Norway, §Department of Animal Ecology, Evolutionary Biology Centre (EBC), Uppsala University, Norbyv€agen 18D, Uppsala 75236, Sweden Dissecting the genetic basis of phenotypic variation in natural populations is a long-standing goal in evolutionary biology. One open question is whether quantitative traits are determined only by large numbers of genes with small effects, or whether variation also exists in large-effect loci. We conducted genomewide association analyses of forehead patch size (a sexually selected trait) on 81 whole-genome-resequenced male collared flycatchers with extreme phenotypes, and on 415 males sampled independent of patch size and genotyped with a 50K SNP chip. No SNPs were genomewide statistically significantly associated with patch size. Simulation-based power analyses suggest that the power to detect large-effect loci responsible for 10% of phenotypic variance was <0.5 in the genome resequencing analysis, and <0.1 in the SNP chip analysis. Reducing the recombination by two-thirds relative to collared flycatchers modestly increased power. Tripling sample size increased power to >0.8 for resequencing of extreme phenotypes (N = 243), but power remained <0.2 for the 50K SNP chip analysis (N = 1245). At least 1 million SNPs were necessary to achieve power >0.8 when analysing 415 randomly sampled phenotypes. However, power of the 50K SNP chip to detect large-effect loci was nearly 0.8 in simulations with a small effective population size of 1500. These results suggest that reliably detecting large-effect trait loci in large natural populations will often require thousands of individuals and near complete sampling of the genome. Encouragingly, far fewer individuals and loci will often be sufficient to reliably detect large-effect loci in small populations with widespread strong linkage disequilibrium.

Keywords: condition-dependent trait, fitness, genomewide association analysis, sexual selection. Understanding the genetic basis of traits that contribute to fitness differences among individuals in natural populations is a long-standing goal in evolutionary biology (Stinchcombe & Hoekstra 2007; Ellegren & Sheldon 2008). Identifying genetic variants associated with fitness traits, and the distribution of their effect sizes, provides clues about the content of the standing genetic variation available for selection to act on. Additionally, identifying associated genes or regulatory sequences with known functions can help to pinpoint the developmental, biochemical and physiological pathways through which selection acting on phenotypes translates into genomic changes over time (Schielzeth & Husby 2014).

The genetic basis of traits closely associated with reproductive performance such as sexually selected traits is of particular interest because such traits may often be influenced by a combination of genes directly involved in trait expression and genes indirectly involved via their effects on condition. Theoretical predictions suggest that variation in condition-dependent, sexually selected traits is likely to be highly polygenic, because of the large number of genes that could affect condition (Rowe & Houle 1996). Empirical data suggest that many sexually selected traits are indeed polygenic, but the distribution Correspondence: Marty Kardos and Hans Ellegren, Fax: 018-471 6310; E-mails: martykardos@gmail.com and hans.ellegren@ebc. uu.se Molecular Ecology Resources (2015) doi: 10.1111/1755-0998.12498 of effect sizes among contributing loci is not well described and seems to be highly variable (Chenoweth & McGuigan 2010; However, relatively few loci have explained a large proportion of variation in some sexually selected traits including eye-stalk length in stalk-eyed flies (Johns et al. 2005) and horn size in Soay sheep (Johnston et al. 2011). Thus, a general understanding of the genetic architecture of sexually selected traits is lacking in natural populations. Until recently, discovering variants contributing to phenotypic variation and fitness (i.e. quantitative trait loci or ‘QTL’) in natural populations has been hindered by the lack of large-scale genomic data on wild individuals. However, genome sequences are accumulating rapidly for nonmodel species (Ellegren 2014), and technologies such as single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping arrays and genotyping by sequencing have made it possible to type many thousands of markers in any species. Yet, attempts to detect QTL in natural populations – where controlled crosses or breeding in captivity are usually not possible – have yielded mixed results, with some studies identifying candidate QTL via genomewide association (GWA) analysis (e.g. Johnston et al. 2011, 2014; Parchman et al. 2012; Comeault et al. 2014; Husby et al. 2015) or pedigree-based linkage mapping (e.g. Johnston et al. 2010; Poissant et al. 2012), and others failing to detect candidate causal variants despite moderately high heritability (Santure et al. 2013). Small sample sizes and small QTL effects sizes are likely reasons for the failure to detect QTL. An additional reason for the failure to detect QTL using association mapping is likely to be that strong linkage disequilibrium (LD) often extends only over short chromosome distances (Fig. 1) (Slatkin 2008), which means the chances of strong associations between marker and trait loci – and thus between marker and phenotype – might be small even when large numbers of genetic markers are used. Whole-genome resequencing has recently become a realistic and increasingly used approach in population genomics (e.g. Ellegren 2014; Lamichhaney et al. 2015). Inspired by this progress, we reasoned that whole-genome resequencing could potentially offer a novel means for mapping trait loci in natural populations. It would imply unprecedented genomic resolution in the search for loci contributing to phenotypic variation in the wild because, in contrast to approaches based on genotyping of even very large sets of SNPs, the problem of low or no LD between the typed markers and causal variants is essentially eliminated by typing nearly all variable sites in the genome. Although large sample sizes may still be necessary to detect candidate loci for traits with polygenic genetic architectures (e.g. Allen et al. 2010), this could potentially be alleviated using the experimental design of sequencing extreme phenotypes. Sampling extreme phenotypes can dramatically reduce the number of individuals necessary to achieve high power relative to studies that sample randomly from the phenotype distribution (Perez-Gracia et al. 2002; Li et al. 2011; Emond et al. 2012; Barnett et al. 2013; Gurwitz & McLeod 2013). For example, Emond et al. (2012) identified a modifier of chronic infection in cystic fibrosis patients using the exome sequences of only 91 individuals with extreme phenotypes. Basically, this approach entails sequencing two groups of individuals – each representing the respective lower and upper tail from the phenotypic distribution, thereby maximizing the phenotypic and genetic variance of the trait of interest among the sampled individuals. Conducting GWA analyses on whole-genome resequencing data by no means ensures that segregating large-effect QTL will be detected (King & Nicolae 2014). The mean minor allele frequency (MAF) is often considerably lower in resequencing data compared to data from SNP chips where the mean MAF is often quite high (Kawakami et al. 2014a,b). The power to detect phenotypic effects is lower at loci with low MAF (King & Nicolae 2014), so increasing the number of loci by adding large numbers of loci with low MAF might not translate Fig. 1 The relationship between the strength of linkage disequilibrium (r2) and physical distance in 81 whole-genome-resequenced collared flycatcher males The data shown are from 250 000 randomly selected SNPs from the 81 whole-genomeresequenced collared flycatchers. r2 was calculated using the –r2 function in PLINK (Purcell et al. 2007) and is shown for each pair of SNPs separated by 50 or fewer kb. The solid line represents a loess function fitted to the rolling mean of r2 calculated in nonoverlapping windows of 100 bp. The dashed lines represent loess functions fitted to the rolling 5% and 95% quantiles of r2 in the same nonoverlapping 100 bp windows. into substantially increased power. Additionally, thresholds for statistical significance of course become more stringent as the number of loci increases, regardless of the MAF of the additional loci. Lastly, sample sizes tend to be limited in whole-genome resequencing studies compared to studies using less-expensive SNP arrays. Lower sample sizes for resequencing-based GWAS means that the power to detect strong QTL effects may be low, even though causal variants are likely to be directly screened for phenotypic effects. Collared flycatchers (Ficedula albicollis) are a cavitynesting, sexually dichromatic species, which breeds in central and eastern Europe, and winters in Southern Africa. They have a mating system where males defend territories and males with higher quality territories tend to have higher reproductive success (P€art 1994). Males have a sexually selected white forehead patch which is used as an honest signal of quality in male–male competition for territories (Qvarnstr€om 1997). Males with large patches tend to be in better condition, win territorial disputes and to produce more offspring than males with smaller patches (Gustafsson et al. 1995; P€art & Qvarnstr€om 1997). Our objective was to test whether sequencing of extreme phenotypes in collared flycatchers could identify loci contributing to variation in forehead patch size in this species. Specifically, we conducted a genomewide association (GWA) analysis of forehead patch size based on whole-genome resequencing of 81 male collared flycatchers sampled from the extreme ends of the phenotypic distribution. We also tested whether we could detect loci associated with forehead patch size using genotypes of 415 males from a custom 50K SNP chip for the collared flycatcher. To our knowledge, this is the first study to use wholegenome resequencing in conjunction with extreme phenotype sampling to study the genetic basis of phenotypic variation in a natural population. Having found no genomewide statistically significantly associated SNPs, we used coalescent simulated genomic data to evaluate the power to detect loci with large phenotypic effects in this study. We also evaluated statistical power of association analyses when using larger sample sizes, and in populations with either a lower recombination rate or smaller effective population size (Ne). Previous work has evaluated the power of pedigree-based QTL linkage mapping methods (Slate 2013). Additionally, the power of GWA analysis for study designs typical of human research has been assessed using simulations (Spencer et al. 2009). Our simulations are motivated by the need to evaluate whether association mapping is likely to detect largeeffect QTL given a range of sample sizes, and genomic and demographic characteristics typical of studies in natural populations.

Sampled individuals and forehead patch size measurements Individuals included in this study were part of a longterm study (2002–2012) on the Baltic island of €Oland (57°100N, 16°580E), where the first breeding pair of collared flycatchers was observed in the 1960s (Qvarnstr€om et al. 2009), although an earlier colonization cannot be excluded. We sampled 81 individuals for GWA analysis based on whole-genome resequencing, and 415 separate individuals for GWA analysis using a 50K SNP chip. To select individuals for sequencing, we first calculated the mean patch size [patch height times patch width (mm)] among all yearly measurements on 819 adult males who were not involved in manipulative experiments that had the potential to influence patch size (e.g. brood size manipulations). We then preferentially selected males from the extreme upper and lower ends of the distribution of mean patch size for sequencing to maximize the phenotypic and genetic variance for patch size among the sequenced individuals. The distribution of patch size measurements is shown for the resequencing and SNP chip typing data sets in Fig. S1 (Supporting information). The mean number of yearly patch size observations per individual among the 81 resequenced males was 2.1 (min. = 1, max. A total of 415 male collared flycatchers were selected independent of patch size and genotyped with a custommade Illumina 50K SNP chip (Kawakami et al. 2014a). The mean number of patch size observations across years among these 415 males was 2.2 (min = 1, max = 7).

Whole-genome resequencing, variant calling and filtering The 81 males selected with extreme phenotypes were subjected to 100 bp paired-end whole-genome resequencing on an Illumina HiSeq instrument. Sequence reads were aligned to the collared flycatcher reference genome assembly version FICALB1.5 (Kawakami et al. 2014b) using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA) (Li & Durbin 2009). We used the Unified Genotyper in the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK, McKenna et al. 2010) to identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) among the whole-genome-resequenced individuals. We applied variant quality score recalibration (VQSR) in GATK, with the top 20% scoring variants used as a training set for quality score recalibration of the remaining variants. We applied a strict tranche sensitivity threshold of 90% when filtering SNPs after VQSR. Filtering loci based on the strict 90% tranche sensitivity threshold selectively removed low MAF SNPs (see Results below).

Repeating the analyses while applying a less stringent tranche sensitivity threshold of 99% did not substantively affect the results (data not shown). We used VCFtools (Danecek et al. 2011) for post variant calling SNP filtering. First, we discarded all genotypes with a genotype quality score ≤20. We then removed SNPs where the minor allele was observed only once, genotypes were missing for ≥4 individuals (i.e. missing in more than approximately 5% of individuals), genotypes deviated significantly (a = 0.01, exact test) from Hardy–Weinberg proportions, or where more than two alleles were present. Sampling extreme phenotypes may enrich the data set for large-effect loci being out of Hardy–Weinberg proportions, where a large number of homozygotes for different alleles could be found in the large- and small-patch samples of individuals. Repeating the analyses without filtering SNPs based on conformation to Hardy–Weinberg proportions did not qualitatively change the results (data not shown). 50K SNP chip genotyping was conducted at the SNP & Seq Technology Platform at Uppsala University (http://www.molmed.medsci.uu.se/SNP+SEQ+Technology+Platform/) on an Illumina iScan instrument. We discarded 50K SNP chip loci with minor allele frequency (MAF) ≤0.01, genotyping rate of <95%, and loci failing a test for Hardy–Weinberg proportions (a = 1.0 9 105). After these filtering steps, 37 803 of 45 183 SNP loci (84%) remained and were used in the GWA analysis.

For GWA analyses, we used linear mixed effects models included as an add-on (RepeatABEL; R€onnegard et al. In press, http://www.genabel.org/packages/RepeatABEL) to the GENABEL package (Aulchenko et al. 2007; Aulchenko et al. 2015) for the program R (R Core Team 2015). The mixed effect models account for both repeated measurements within individuals and relatedness among individuals. Specifically, we fitted a linear mixed effects model of the form where X is the design matrix for nongenetic fixed effects (age and year of sampling) and b are the corresponding fixed effects. XSNP is the design matrix for the SNP genotype predictor (coded 0, 1 or 2) and bSNP are the corresponding SNP effects. g is a random genetic effect, p is a permanent environmental effect for each individual, and e is the error term. Patch size has been shown to increase with age (P€art & Qvarnstr€om 1997), and age was thus included as a fixed effect in our GWA analyses. Year of sampling was also included as a fixed effect to account for the effects of temporal environmental fluctuations on patch size (Fig. S2, Supporting information). Simultaneously including SNPs with large phenotypic effects in the fixed effects (i.e. to estimate the individual SNP effects) and in the random effects by including them when estimating the genetic relatedness matrix can result in reduced power to detect effects of individual SNPs (Yang et al. 2014). Therefore, we repeated the GWA analyses and ran the analyses separately for each chromosome. For GWA analysis of each chromosome, we estimated the genetic relatedness matrix using SNPs on all of the chromosomes other than the chromosome included in the GWA analysis. The analysis did not substantively affect the results (data not shown). The P-values reported from GWA analyses are from Wald tests and are corrected for relatedness among individuals, repeated measurements and genomic inflation (see below). We estimated the narrow sense heritability (h2) of patch size from GWA analyses as where Va is the additive genetic variance, Vpe is the permanent among-individual variance due to environmental differences, and Ve is residual error variance.

Stringent thresholds of statistical significance are necessary to control the probability of false positive genotype– phenotype associations. The simplest approaches to correct for multiple tests such as Bonferroni correction and false discovery rate techniques are overly conservative in GWA studies such as this one where SNP density is high and many SNPs are in substantial LD. Genotype– phenotype tests at closely linked SNPs are in such cases nonindependent (Clarke et al. 2011). Therefore, to determine whether the chosen type of statistical correction affected the results, we used both a Bonferroni correction and a permutation approach that accounts for LD among closely linked loci (Clarke et al. 2011) and controls the probability of a single false positive occurring. For the permutation approach, we repeated the GWA analysis as described above 1000 times, each time after randomly reassigning patch size measurements among individuals. We saved the P-value from each of the 2 039 641 genotype–phenotype association tests on each randomized data set. This was performed to derive the distribution of P-values expected when no SNPs are truly related to patch size. We then identified the statistical significance threshold for the empirical GWA analysis as the P-value below which a single false positive was identified in 5% or fewer of the randomized data sets. The threshold of statistical significance determined with permutation for the GWA analyses of the whole-genome-resequenced individuals was P = 1.002 9 107. Many of the 50K SNP chip loci were in substantial LD in our study population (Kawakami et al. 2014a). Thus, we used the same permutation approach as described above as well as a Bonferroni correction to control for multiple testing in the GWA analysis of these data. Here, the threshold of statistical significance determined by permutation was P = 2.18 9 106.

We corrected P-values from GWA analyses for genomic inflation by dividing the test statistic (v2) by the genomic inflation factor (k). k was estimated as the slope from a regression of observed v2 vs. expected v2 assuming that patch size was not affected by variation at any loci. This approach is conservative because genomic inflation is expected in GWA studies involving highly polygenic traits (Yang et al. 2011), which is very likely the case for sexually selected traits (Rowe & Houle 1996) such as patch size in collared flycatchers. However, repeating the analyses without correcting for genomic inflation did not qualitatively change the results (data not shown).

Simulations to evaluate power to detect QTL for patch size We used coalescent simulations to evaluate the power to detect loci with large effects on patch size. We simulated genomic data with FASTSIMCOAL2 v. 2.5.1 (Excoffier et al. 2013). We tested a range of values for the simulated Ne, and recombination and mutation rates to identify a set of parameter values that resulted in a LD pattern similar to the empirical data (Fig. S3, Supporting information). We simulated populations with constant diploid Ne = 37 500. Recombination and mutation rates were set to 3.1 9 108 (Kawakami et al. 2014b), and 5.0 9 109 (Ellegren 2007) per bp per generation, respectively. For computational efficiency, we simulated only two single 200 kb chromosomes in each population. Chromosomes of this size are sufficient because LD is substantially greater than the genomic background level only for markers separated by less than approximately 10–20 kb in our study population (Fig. 1; Kawakami et al. 2014a) and in the simulated data (Fig. S3, Supporting information). We generated 1500 diploid individuals from each simulation repetition by randomly pairing 3000 simulated haploid chromosomes. We used RepeatABEL to simulate a normally distributed quantitative trait associated with SNP variation among the 1500 individuals sampled from each simulated population. The number of simulated repeated measurements per individual was selected randomly from the empirical distribution of measurements among the 81 whole-genome-resequenced individuals. The simulations assumed the variance components estimated from the SNP chip-based GWA analysis (Table 1). We used these variance components because RepeatABEL simulates a normally distributed quantitative trait and the distribution of the phenotypes in the SNP chip-based empirical analysis was approximately normal. For each simulated population, the phenotype was associated with a single SNP having a MAF of at least 0.2 as close as possible to the physical centre of the first chromosome. Our simulations therefore assume that QTL effects are due to common variants, which are more easily detected than rare variants. We varied the genotypic effect of the simulated QTL (a = half the expected phenotypic difference between homozygotes) so that the additive genetic variance attributed to the QTL (Vqtl) was equal to 5, 10, 15 and 20% of the total phenotypic variance (Vp, which was set equal to the total phenotype variance from the empirical SNP chip-based GWA analysis described above), respectively. We determined values of a by solving the expression Vqtl = 2pqa2 (where p and q are the frequencies of the minor and major allele, respectively, Lynch & Walsh (1998)) for a, after setting Vqtl equal to 0.05, 0.1, 0.15 or 0.2 times Vp. For each simulation, the simulated polygenic additive genetic variance (Va*) was set to Va* = Va – Vqtl, where Va is the empirical estimate of the polygenic additive genetic variance, so that the total and additive genetic components of variance in the simulated phenotype was representative of the empirical data, and held constant across all of the simulations. We consider these simulated effect sizes to be large, as they account for approximately 1/6 to 2/3 of the total heritability of the simulated phenotype. To evaluate the power to detect QTL in the sample of individuals with extreme phenotypes, we randomly sampled 81 individuals from the upper (46 individuals) Table 1 Variance component estimates from GWA analyses. 95% confidence intervals calculated in RepeatABEL are provided in parentheses Whole Genome (N = 81) 251.67 (161.4, 392.5) 171.91 (102.1,289.5) 101.82 (75.6, 137.1) 50K SNP Chip (N = 415) 69.82 (55.8, 87.4) 57.43 (45.4, 72.7) 88.45 (79.2, 98.8) DETECTING QTL IN NATURAL POPULATIONS 5 and lower (35 individuals) 10% quantiles of mean simulated patch size. We randomly subsampled SNPs on the first simulated chromosome (where the simulated QTL was located) without including singletons, so that SNP density was equal to the empirical whole-genome resequencing data after filtering steps. The loci were randomly selected using the sample function in R, with the probability of a SNP being selected weighted by the squared MAF so that the least variable loci would be selectively removed as in our analysis of the empirical resequencing data. We defined power as the proportion of simulations where any SNP located on the first chromosome was statistically significantly associated with phenotype after correcting for multiple tests (see below). We used the same simulated populations as above to evaluate the power to detect QTL in the 415 males with 50K SNP chip genotypes. Here, we randomly selected 415 simulated diploid individuals for analysis of each simulation. For the GWA analyses of these simulated data, we randomly subsampled SNPs so that marker density was as close as possible to the average density observed in the empirical GWA analyses based on the SNP chip. The SNP chip loci had a relatively high mean MAF of 0.28 (SD = 0.13). Therefore, we preferentially selected high MAF loci from the simulated data to maximize the power of SNP chip GWA analysis of the simulated data. We achieved this in the same way as above for the simulated analyses of the resequencing data using the sample function in R to randomly select SNPs after weighting the selection probabilities by the squared MAF. We repeated the GWA analyses of simulations of the 415 males after subsampling SNPs as described above so that the marker densities were equivalent to 50K, 100K, 250K, 500K, 1 and 2 million SNPs (nearly equivalent to SNP density in our whole-genome resequencing data set) in the flycatcher genome assembly to evaluate the effects of marker density on power to detect QTL. We again defined power as the proportion of simulations where one or more SNPs located on chromosome one were statistically significantly associated with the simulated phenotype after correcting for multiple tests. We ran the GWA analyses on the simulated data for power analysis as described above for the empirical data. However, there were a few necessary exceptions. First, age and year of sampling were not simulated and were therefore not included as fixed effects in GWA analyses of simulated data for power analysis. Additionally, initial testing showed that the power to detect simulated large-effect QTL was reduced when the QTL and linked SNPs were used to estimate the GRM [consistent with the findings of Yang et al. Therefore, in the analyses presented below, we estimated the GRM using only the loci on the second chromosome (i.e. only using SNPs that were not linked to the simulated QTL). We used all of the simulated SNPs on the second chromosome (690 loci on average) to estimate the GRM. This approximates the general scenario where a candidate QTL region is excluded from estimation of the GRM, and a large number of loci unlinked to the candidate region are used to estimate the GRM and thus to account for polygenic effects and relatedness among the sampled individuals. We evaluated statistical power using statistical significance thresholds ranging from very conservative to very liberal. Using permutation on each simulated data set was unreasonable due to the enormous computational requirements. We determined ‘conservative’ adjusted a values by applying the same Bonferroni-corrected statistical significance thresholds as in the empirical analyses so that the power estimates would reflect the probability of detecting large-effect QTL in our empirical data. The Bonferroni-adjusted a values were determined by dividing 0.05 by 2 039 641 when evaluating the power of the analysis of whole-genome-resequenced individuals with extreme phenotypes. We divided 0.05 by each of the number of loci of interest (37.8K, 50K, 100K, 250K, 500K, 1 and 2 million SNPs) when evaluating the power of the SNP chip-based GWA analysis of patch size. To derive ‘moderate’ and ‘liberal’ adjusted statistical significance threshold values, we multiplied the Bonferroni-corrected statistical significance thresholds by 5 and 10, respectively. We then estimated statistical power using the conservative, moderate and liberal adjusted statistical significance thresholds.

Effects of sample size, recombination rate and effective population size on power of GWA analyses The power of GWA analyses is expected to be higher with increased sample size and in populations where strong LD extends over longer chromosomal distances. To extend inferences related to power beyond our empirical study, we evaluated power to detect QTL with GWA analyses in simulated populations with a lower recombination rate and small Ne. We also evaluated the effects on power of increasing the sample size by three times compared to our empirical study. The pattern of LD in collared flycatchers (Fig. 1) is not representative of all populations where GWA analyses will be performed in the future. The relatively large Ne and a high recombination rate [3.1 cM/Mb on average, (Kawakami et al. 2014b)] in the collared flycatcher act to reduce the chromosomal distance over which strong LD extends compared to smaller populations, or populations with lower recombination rates. Note, however, that LD is expected to extend even shorter distances in populations with larger Ne (e.g. as in some invertebrates). We conducted power analyses using simulated populations with recombination rate of 1.03 cM/Mb (1/3 times the recombination rate in collared flycatchers, Kawakami et al. 2014b), which is typical of the distribution of recombination rates among mammals (Dumont & Payseur 2008). We also ran power analyses on simulated populations with diploid Ne = 1500, assuming a higher mutation rate of l = 2 9 107 to ensure enough polymorphic sites for the GWA analyses of these data to be comparable to the analyses of simulated populations with larger Ne. The physical size of the simulated chromosomes was increased to 600 kb for simulations with low recombination rate and for simulations with small Ne to accommodate the increased extent of strong LD in these scenarios (Fig. S3, Supporting information). We held all other simulation parameters the same as before. We ran the GWA and power analyses on the simulated populations with lower recombination or smaller Ne as described above.

A total of 81 male collared flycatchers were resequenced to a mean genomewide coverage of 18.4 X (range 9.6– 27.0 X) and mapped to a repeat-masked version of the 1.1 Gb reference assembly of the collared flycatcher genome. We applied highly stringent filters for the inclusion of sites in variant identification by requesting that a genotype had been called for ≥95% of all individuals. After VQSR (with tranche sensitivity threshold of 90%) and discarding singletons, 2 017 971 SNPs remained (1 906 598 SNPs on autosomes and 111 373 SNPs on the Z chromosome) with mean MAF of 0.29 (SD = 0.13). Analysis of the resequencing data was repeated using a less stringent tranche sensitivity threshold of 99% in the VQSR; this less stringent filtering resulted in 4 376 065 SNPs remaining with mean MAF = 0.20 (SD = 0.13). We also repeated the analysis of the resequencing data using SNPs called for ≥90% of all individuals; this filtering resulted in 2 777 500 SNPs remaining after filtering. The repeated analyses applying tranche sensitivity threshold of 99%, and retaining SNPs called in ≥90% of all individuals did not substantively affect the results (data not shown). The strict tranche sensitivity threshold of 90% preferentially removed low MAF SNPs from the data set. The resulting high mean MAF means that the power to detect QTL was maximized for the given number of SNPs distributed across the genome.

No SNP was genomewide statistically significantly associated with patch size in the analysis of wholegenome-resequenced males. The two SNPs with the lowest P-values were located 14 bp apart within a large intergenic region located on chromosome 2 (Fig. 2 and Fig. S4, Supporting information). The closest annotated gene to these SNPs (CSMD3) was located ~300 kb away. The GWA analysis indicated genomic inflation of the test statistic (k = 1.11; Fig. S5, Supporting information). The genomic estimate of patch size heritability in the wholegenome-resequenced males was h2=0.48.

There were also no SNPs genomewide statistically significantly associated with patch size in the analysis of SNP chip-genotyped males (Fig. 2). There was little genomic inflation in this analysis (k = 1.02; Fig. S5, Supporting information). The genomic estimate of heritability was h2 = 0.32. The values of h2 from analyses of whole-genome-resequenced and SNP chip-genotyped males are in the range of estimates based on previous pedigree-based analyses (Qvarnstr€om 1999). There were no SNPs that simultaneously had exceptionally low P-values in the GWA analyses of whole-genome resequencing and SNP chip data sets (Fig. S6, Supporting information). Further, the P-values from the SNP chip- and resequencing-based GWA analyses were not even weakly correlated (r2 < 0.01). Variance component estimates with 95% confidence intervals from each analysis are shown in Table 1.

Our simulations suggested that the power to detect QTL with large effects was insufficient in both of the empirical analyses (Fig. 3a, Figs S7 and S8, Supporting information). The results presented here in the main text are from analyses that used a medium statistical significance threshold. The results from analyses that applied Bonferroni and liberal statistical significance thresholds are presented in detail in Figs S7 and S8 (Supporting information). Power was high (>0.8) only in the case of extreme phenotype sampling with whole-genome resequencing when Vqtl/Vp was ≥0.15. The power to detect QTL with effect sizes of Vqtl/Vp = 0.05 and Vqtl/ Vp = 0.10 in our whole-genome resequencing analysis was then 0.06 and 0.44, respectively. The power to detect QTL with effect sizes of Vqtl/Vp = 0.05 and Vqtl/Vp = 0.2 in our analysis of the 415 SNP chip-genotyped individuals sampled independent of phenotype was 0.06 and 0.13, respectively. The relationship between GWA analysis P-values and physical distance from the simulated QTL with effect size of Vqtl/Vp = 0.05 is shown in Fig. The great majority of SNPs closely linked to the simulated QTL were not close to being statistically significantly associated with phenotype. For example, the median P-value DETECTING QTL IN NATURAL POPULATIONS 7 for SNPs located within 1 kb of the simulated QTL among 1,000 simulations of 81 whole-genome-resequenced individuals with extreme phenotypes was P = 0.15, which is eight orders of magnitude larger than the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of statistical significance for the GWA analyses of resequenced individuals (2.5 9 108). The median P-value for SNPs within 1 kb of the QTL in simulations of 415 individuals sampled independent of patch size was P = was 0.084, which is four orders of magnitude larger than the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of statistical significance for the SNP chip-based GWA analysis (1.3 9 106).

Effects of number of loci, sample size, recombination rate and Ne on power to detect QTL The number of loci used in the SNP chip scenario had a strong effect on statistical power. However, using hundreds of thousands or millions of SNPs did not ensure that power was high (Fig. 3a). For example, power with 100K and 500K SNPs was <0.3 and 0.75, respectively, for all simulated QTL effect sizes. Power to detect QTL with effect size of Vqtl/Vp = 0.05 was <0.5 when using 2 million SNPs. At least 1 million SNPs were necessary to achieve power of 0.8 or higher for QTL with effect sizes of Vqtl/Vp = 0.15 or 0.2 in this scenario (N = 415 individuals, Fig. 3a). Tripling the sample size (N = 243) substantially increased the power to detect large-effect QTL in the simulations of whole-genome resequencing of extreme phenotypes (Fig. 3b). Specifically, power was >0.8 for all simulated effect sizes, and 100% of QTL with effect size of Vqtl/Vp ≥0.1 were detected. Power was >0.9 for all QTL effect sizes in the simulations of the SNP chip scenario when 1–2 million SNPs were used and the sample sizes were tripled to N = 1245 (Fig. 3b). However, power was quite low (<0.4) for all QTL effect sizes when 100 K or fewer SNPs were used and the sample sizes were tripled. Next, we evaluated the effects on power of increased LD due to lower recombination rate (1.03 cM/Mb instead of 3.1 cM/Mb) in the simulated populations. Our analyses revealed no genomewide significant loci for variation in male forehead patch size, despite moderate narrow sense heritability and typing nearly all polymorphic sites in the genome in 81 individuals with extreme phenotypes. However, as discussed below, low power of the GWA analyses of patch size means we cannot confidently conclude that large-effect loci for patch size were not present.

Our results suggest that patch size had moderately high heritability. We found higher estimated narrow sense heritability of patch size in the analysis of whole-genome-resequenced individuals with extreme phenotypes (h2 = 0.48) than for SNP chip-genotyped individuals sampled independent of patch size (h2 = 0.31). This difference in h2 between analyses is likely due to an enrichment of the genetic variance in patch size in the group of sampled individuals with extreme phenotypes. Thus, the strategy of sampling extreme phenotypes appears to have been successful in maximizing the additive genetic variance for the trait and thus increased the power of this analysis relative to analyses based on individuals sampled randomly with respect to patch size. However, this difference could be due to a lower number of whole- genome-resequenced males (81) compared to SNP chip-genotyped males (415). Indeed, the number of samples has been found to have stronger effects than the number of typed sites on the precision of h2 estimates (Stanton-Geddes et al. 2013). Nevertheless, both estimates of heritability suggest that patch size is considerably heritable.

The inference of the absence of large-effect SNPs for patch size assumes that we would have detected loci with large effects on patch size if they existed. We sampled 81 males from the ends of the distribution of patch size distribution to enrich for total and additive genetic variance of patch size, thus maximizing power given the number of individuals available for sequencing (Gurwitz & McLeod 2013). Whole-genome sequencing of these males means that essentially all SNPs in the genome were screened, thereby nearly eliminating the problem of low or no LD between the typed SNPs and causal loci. SNP chip typing a larger number of samples (415) as in the analysis of males selected independent of patch size is expected to reduce the sampling error of estimated SNP effects at the typed loci. Additionally, using a low-density SNP chip means that only a very small fraction of the genome was effectively screened for phenotypic effects because strong LD extended <10–20 kb in our study population (Fig. 1). Our power analyses suggest that the power to detect large-effect QTL was low in all cases, even when the causal loci were directly screened for genotype–phenotype associations (Figs 3a and 4a). Thus, the power analyses suggest that our empirical data were not sufficient to confidently determine whether SNPs with large effects on patch size segregated in the study population. The power analysis results presented here should be useful to future attempts to dissect the genetic basis of complex traits in natural populations. First, the problem of very low LD between typed markers and the great majority of functional positions in the genomes is likely to be characteristic of many studies on natural populations in the future. The distance over which strong LD persists is determined by Ne (the strength of genetic drift), historical fluctuations in population size, population subdivision, population admixture and the recombination rate (Slatkin 2008). Thus, genomic patterns of LD vary considerably among species and populations. For example, strong LD extends over large chromosomal distances in humans (Reich et al. 2001), domesticated sheep and cattle (McKay et al. 2007; Meadows et al. 2008) and three-spined sticklebacks (Hohenlohe et al. 2012). However, LD decays much more rapidly in the collared flycatcher (Kawakami et al. 2014a) (Fig. 1), and invertebrates such as the nematode Caenorhabditis remanei (Cutter et al. 2006), the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster (Mackay et al. 2012) and the mosquito Anopheles arabiensis (Marsden et al. 2014). Rapid decay of LD with increasing chromosomal distance means that QTL are more difficult to detect via association analyses of linked SNPs. However, the flipside of this problem is that causal variants are more difficult to pinpoint within QTL regions in species with low recombination rates or small Ne where genotype–phenotype correlations may be due to causal variants located far away from genotyped loci (Fig. 4b). Our results suggest that it will often be necessary to have many SNPs very closely linked to a QTL with large effects to reliably detect its phenotypic effects (Figs 3 and 4), particularly in populations where strong LD extends over only short distances. We suggest that extremely high marker density (approaching whole-genome sequence) and very large samples will often be necessary to reliably detect QTLs in populations with weak LD (e.g. due to high recombination rates or large Ne). However, investing in whole-genome resequencing will result in smaller increases in power to detect QTL compared to very high density SNP genotyping approaches in study systems with low recombination rate and/or small Ne and thus strong LD extending over larger chromosome segments (Figs 3 and 4). A notable result of the simulation-based power analyses is that the power to detect a large-effect QTL (e.g. Vqtl/Vp = 0.1) can be low when the causal SNP itself is directly screened for a genotype–phenotype association (Fig. 4). Clearly, this is caused by relatively small sample sizes and adjusting statistical significance thresholds to correct for multiple testing. For example, P-values smaller than 2.5 9 108 are necessary to identify candidate QTL when 2 million loci are used in a GWA analysis and a standard Bonferroni correction is applied along with an a value of 0.05. Thus, having every SNP in the genome genotyped means that the sample sizes may often need to be very large for large-effect QTLs to consistently surpass reasonable statistical significance thresholds. However, as our simulations (Fig. 3) and other results from humans (Perez-Gracia et al. 2002; Li et al. 2011; Emond et al. 2012; Barnett et al. 2013; Gurwitz & McLeod 2013) demonstrate, sampling from the ends of the distribution of phenotypes can dramatically decrease the number of individuals necessary to achieve high power. Resequencing of samples from the ends of the phenotype distribution is therefore a promising approach to identify the genetic basis of phenotypic and fitness variation in natural populations where budgets and sample sizes are often small.

Several affordable and relatively large-scale genotyping technologies including genotyping-by-sequencing and SNP genotyping arrays have emerged in the last several years, making it possible to genotype thousands to hundreds of thousands of SNPs in any organism (Allendorf et al. 2010; There has been much excitement about the potential for new genotyping or genotyping-by-sequencing technologies to help elucidate the genetic basis of phenotypic and fitness variation in natural populations (Slate et al. 2009; Stapley et al. 2010). However, the simulations here along with previous results (Spencer et al. 2009) suggest that reliable detection of QTL with large effect sizes will often require on the order of several hundred thousand SNPs or wholegenome sequence, along with very large sample sizes to reliably detect large effect size QTL with GWA analyses. Thus, it may be the case that subgenome scale genomic data will be insufficient to reliably detect large-effect QTLs in many other study systems where LD decays rapidly. A notable result from our simulations is the dramatically higher power of GWA analyses based on relatively DETECTING QTL IN NATURAL POPULATIONS 11 few loci (e.g. 50K-100K SNPs) in populations with small Ne (Figs 3d and 4b). This suggests that the prospects are good for detecting large-effect QTL in populations with small Ne where LD is likely to extend over very large distances (e.g. in long-term studies of isolated populations on habitat islands). Our simulations of small populations assumed Ne = 1500 and a recombination rate of 3.1 cM/ Mb. Populations with smaller Ne and/or lower recombination rates are expected to have strong LD extending over longer distances than in these simulations. Therefore, power to detect large-effect QTL with GWA analyses based on tens of thousands of SNPs and sample sizes only in the hundreds may be quite high in some study populations. The genomic pattern of LD has been described in detail in relatively few nonmodel species. Given its importance for the development of efficient tools for the detection of the genomic basis of phenotypic and fitness variation, describing LD in detail in taxa where fitness and phenotypic data are accumulating will greatly aid in the efforts to identify QTLs in these species. We suggest that future GWA studies should report the genomic pattern of LD and estimates of power to detect large-effect QTL and interpret results in the light of whether power is likely to be high or low given the observed pattern of LD and the sampling design. Clearly, if LD is weak and few SNPs are used for GWA analyses, only a small fraction of the genome can be effectively scanned for QTL, and therefore, QTL with even very large phenotypic effects will frequently be missed. Nevertheless, QTL have been detected via GWA analysis in natural populations using small numbers of loci. For example, a recent GWA analysis of parasite burden in red grouse (Lagopus lagopus scotica) based on only 271 SNPs identified 5 genomewide statistically significant QTL (Wenzel et al. 2015). How can the low power of GWA association analyses using sparse SNPs be reconciled with the successful identification of candidate QTL in such studies? One possibility is of course that many of the QTL reported in highly underpowered studies (e.g. where only hundreds to a few thousand SNPs are typed in large genomes) represent false positives, because very low power means that a large proportion of positive results are expected to be false (Christley 2010). Ideally, reported QTL should be replicated in an independent sample(s), although this is not always possible in studies on natural populations. As a result of low power in combination with a possible bias towards publication of positive results, false positives could be overrepresented in the literature. Alternatively, underpowered GWA analyses may frequently detect a small number of true QTL [usually overestimating their effect sizes, G€oring et al. due to the presence of a large number of QTL with individually small effects if the trait is polygenic. In either case, both of these scenarios will not substantially advance our understanding of the genetic basis of quantitative traits in natural populations. Identifying a handful of QTL that together explain a tiny fraction of trait heritability is of limited use because many other undetected genes and biochemical pathways are involved but overlooked. Indeed, focusing interpretation of results on the functions of a few small-effect QTL that happen to reach statistical significance is likely to provide a biased view of the genetic and biochemical mechanisms underpinning trait variation. Insufficient power to detect large-effect QTL has other important implications for investigations into the genetic basis of phenotypic and fitness variation in natural populations. For example, one question of great interest in evolutionary biology is whether quantitative traits are generally governed by a very large number of genes with individually small effects or whether a substantial proportion of variation is due to large effects of a small number of genes. As demonstrated here, caution is required in interpreting the apparent absence of largeeffect loci as evidence for a polygenic architecture of quantitative trait variation if power to detect QTL is low. Low power to detect large-effect QTL also makes it difficult to rigorously compare the genetic architecture of different traits within natural populations. Describing architectural differences in such traits is important for our understanding of how standing genetic variation affects different traits and how these traits might respond to selection. Large-effect loci may be detected for some traits while QTL with similarly large effects are not detected for other traits of interest. We emphasize that it should clearly be acknowledged that apparent differences in the genetic architectures of different traits may be caused by low power to detect large-effect QTL, rather than differences in the distribution of effect sizes of QTL among different phenotypic characteristics or fitness components. Pedigree-based QTL linkage mapping studies might often have higher power than GWA approaches to detect large-effect QTL because LD will obviously extend over longer chromosomal distances within families than in samples of unrelated individuals typical of GWA studies (Schielzeth & Husby 2014). Indeed, candidate QTL have been detected via linkage mapping (e.g. Johnston et al. 2010; Poissant et al. 2012), with some studies involving controlled crosses (Laporte et al. 2015) or breeding in captivity (Knief et al. 2012; However, previous simulations suggest that the power to detect large-effect QTL has been quite low (e.g. power was estimated at 0.33 for QTL explaining >10% of phenotypic variance) in some of the most powerful linkage mapping studies carried out to date (Slate 2013). Another limiting factor is that multiple generation pedigrees are only available in few study systems, thus limiting the usefulness of pedigree-based QTL mapping to relatively few species and phenotypic traits. Potentially increased power due to longer range LD is balanced by decreased precision in pinpointing causal loci among those linked to identified QTL. A more general understanding of the genetic basis of phenotypic and fitness variation in natural populations will likely require application of very large-scale genotyping or sequencing technologies in GWA studies of large samples of individuals in many natural populations representing a broad diversity of taxa and evolutionary histories. Fortunately, this goal is becoming within reach as the repertoire of genomic resources available for nonmodel organisms expands rapidly (Ellegren 2014).
